questions.title: What is the practical and legal effect of vacating prior stays and issuing a new stay pending appeal?
questions.question_body: The Ninth Circuit vacated its March 25 stay (as amended) and its July 18 administrative stay, then issued a new stay pending appeal that keeps most of the district court's injunctions stayed except for a directive to reinstate cooperative agreements for reception and placement services. How do administrative stays differ from stays pending appeal, and why would vacating prior stays make the government's July 17 emergency motion "moot"? Also, what authority does an appellate panel have to tailor a new stay to include affirmative obligations (like reinstating agreements) while generally staying the injunction?

questions.title: Can the President suspend refugee admissions under 8 U.S.C. § 1182(f) despite the Refugee Act’s specific admissions framework?
questions.question_body: The panel relies on Trump v. Hawaii to conclude the President is likely to prevail on the legality of suspending refugee admissions under § 1182(f), saying courts cannot engage in a searching inquiry into his justifications. But the Refugee Act (8 U.S.C. § 1157 et seq.) sets out a detailed process for determining refugee admissions and consultations with Congress. How do courts reconcile the broad § 1182(f) "suspend entry" power with this specific statutory scheme? Is there any argument that the Refugee Act implicitly cabins § 1182(f) when it comes to refugee admissions, or is Hawaii read to foreclose that?

questions.title: Are the State Department’s terminations of refugee cooperative agreements reviewable under the APA, and can a court order reinstatement?
questions.question_body: Plaintiffs challenge the defunding and termination of cooperative agreements as violating the APA. The order suggests the government is unlikely to prevail on at least one APA claim tied to 8 U.S.C. § 1522 and directs reinstatement of cooperative agreements necessary to provide services to admitted refugees. My confusion: (1) Is the EO itself reviewable under the APA, or must plaintiffs target discrete "final agency action" like State's termination notices? (2) What APA theories fit here—contrary to law (if § 1522 mandates services), arbitrary and capricious for failing to consider reliance or statutory factors, or procedural defects? (3) Is reinstatement of terminated agreements an available APA remedy, or does that cross into nonreviewable contract/procurement discretion?

questions.title: Does 8 U.S.C. § 1522 mandate refugee services or merely authorize them, especially given the title "Authorization" and the use of "shall"?
questions.question_body: The majority reads § 1522 as imposing mandatory duties (citing § 1522(a)(1)(A), (d)(2)(B), and (e)(7)(A)), while Judge Lee argues the statute is primarily permissive: the title says "Authorization," subsections (b)-(e) use "is authorized," and the "shall" language in § 1522(a) is just a condition that applies only if the government chooses to fund programs. How do courts interpret the interplay between a section title signaling authorization and operative text using "shall" with qualifiers like "to the extent of available appropriations," "if necessary," and "as needed"? Are there canons or precedents specific to reconciling these mixed signals within § 1522?

questions.title: Can the Executive suspend or withhold refugee-related funds that Congress has appropriated, consistent with the Impoundment Control Act?
questions.question_body: The order notes Congress appropriated several billion dollars for migration and refugee assistance in FY 2025, with a partial rescission. Yet the State Department suspended all USRAP funding and terminated cooperative agreements, purportedly under an EO reevaluating foreign aid. Is this a lawful "programmatic delay" or does it raise an impoundment issue if the Executive withholds or delays funds for policy reasons? Do different rules apply to State Department foreign assistance funds versus HHS’s ORR funds, and how might those distinctions matter for APA or statutory claims?

questions.title: Which agency’s programs fall under § 1522, and does that statute actually govern State Department reception and placement agreements?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites § 1522 and ORR obligations (HHS), but the historical "Reception and Placement" program (R&P) is run by the State Department’s Bureau of Population, Refugees, and Migration under the Migration and Refugee Assistance appropriation. The panel then orders reinstatement of State’s cooperative agreements "necessary to provide the reception and placement services described in § 1522." Is § 1522 properly read to govern State’s R&P cooperative agreements, or does it primarily govern ORR’s domestic assistance programs? If State’s R&P is under separate authority, what is the legal hook for compelling State to reinstate those agreements based on § 1522?

questions.title: Do refugees abroad and resettlement organizations have standing and fall within the zone of interests to challenge a § 1182(f) suspension and funding terminations?
questions.question_body: Plaintiffs include refugees admitted to the U.S., refugees conditionally approved but still abroad, and organizations with cooperative agreements. For those still outside the U.S., do they have standing to challenge entry suspensions after Trump v. Hawaii? For the organizational plaintiffs, does the APA’s zone-of-interests test allow them to invoke § 1522 or related provisions to challenge termination of their agreements, or are such claims too attenuated or contractual in nature?

questions.title: What is the legal basis for the panel’s earlier carveout for conditionally approved refugees and the district court’s appointment of a magistrate to oversee compliance?
questions.question_body: Earlier, the motions panel carved out from the stay individuals conditionally approved for refugee status before Jan. 20, 2025, and the district court then set an enforcement framework and appointed a magistrate judge to oversee it. On what authority can an appellate court tailor a stay with such a carveout, and what standard governs district court managerial orders (like appointing a magistrate or special master) to administer that carveout while the merits are on appeal? Does such supervision risk contravening the stay or exceed ancillary enforcement powers?
